title: State (BSES YPL) v. Mohd. Riyaz & Anr.
court: Addl. Sessions Judge-05 (Electricity), East, Karkardooma Courts, Delhi
result: Mohd. Riyaz (user) convicted u/s 135; Firoza Begum (wife, registered consumer) convicted u/s 135 r/w 150 (abetment); civil liability settled during trial but amount not deposited; posted for hearing on sentence

interpretations.interpretation: 'Consumer' covers both the person actually using the electricity and the owner/registered consumer of the connected premises; a registered consumer cannot disown liability for illegal abstraction found at her premises merely because another (her son) was the user (Lokesh Chandela followed).

Drawing supply through an illegal wire connected into the supply cable while the installed meter lies stopped — the service cable tampered so consumption bypasses registration — is direct theft; the stopped meter, tampered cable and absence of any lawful-source explanation evidence the dishonest design (s.24 IPC standard).

The compulsory presumption arises on proof of an artificial/unauthorised means and operates against the user AND the registered consumer alike; each must rebut on the prudent-man standard, the natural mode being proof of lawful metered use (paid bills; s.106 Evidence Act onus).

A registered consumer who, knowing her meter is lying stopped, permits or consciously allows the user to draw supply through an unauthorised connection abets the theft; under s.150(1) the abettor incurs the same punishment as the principal offence, notwithstanding anything in the IPC.

Inspection power with photo-ID safeguards (60); contemporaneous report, seizure/sealing, video documentation (61); prosecution only where dishonest intention evident, disconnection + police complaint within 24 hours, missing seal alone insufficient (62); assessment at twice tariff for up to 12 months with credit for paid units (63). Unchallenged compliance confirms regularity.

citations.case: Sonu @ Amar v. State of Haryana
citations.principle: Objection to want of a Section 65B certificate goes to the mode of proof and must be raised when the electronic record is tendered; if not taken at trial it cannot be raised later.

citations.case: Lokesh Chandela v. State of NCT & Ors.
citations.principle: Both user and owner/registered consumer fall within 'consumer' under Section 2(15); registered consumer answerable for illegal abstraction found at the premises.

citations.case: Punjab State Electricity Board v. Ashwani Kumar
citations.principle: Official inspection report carries a presumption of regularity; onus on the consumer to rebut by cogent evidence.

citations.case: Sushil Sharma v. BSES Rajdhani Power Ltd.
citations.principle: Non-examination of an independent/public witness is no infirmity where inspecting officials are trustworthy and bear no enmity.
'Shall presume' denotes a compulsory legal presumption the court is bound to draw until disproved.

citations.case: Hiten P. Dalal v. Bratindranath Banerjee
citations.principle: Rebuttal of a statutory presumption need not be conclusive; evidence must make the defence reasonably probable to a prudent man.

citations.case: Mukesh Rastogi v. North Delhi Power Ltd.
citations.principle: Easiest rebuttal of the theft presumption is production of paid electricity bills; Section 106 Evidence Act places that onus on the consumer.

significance.point: A stopped meter with a live load is itself the case to answer
significance.explanation: Where the meter reads stopped and the premises visibly consume power through a tampered service cable, the burden effectively shifts to the occupants to show a lawful source — and silence convicts.

significance.point: Registered consumers cannot hide behind the actual user
significance.explanation: Section 2(15) reaches the non-user registered consumer; knowing permission of theft at her premises is abetment u/s 150 carrying the principal's punishment (Lokesh Chandela).

significance.point: Appearing in the inspection video demands an explanation
significance.explanation: The accused's unexplained presence in the videography — whose genuineness he never disputed — undercut the plea that no inspection took place; the missing 65B certificate did not help absent a timely objection (Sonu @ Amar).

significance.point: The reverse-onus presumption binds both accused
significance.explanation: Once the unauthorised means is proved, only evidence of lawful metered use (paid bills; s.106 onus, Mukesh Rastogi) rebuts the presumption — for user and registered consumer alike.

significance.point: Settlement corroborates guilt even if never paid
significance.explanation: Settling the theft bill while pleading inability to deposit was read as conduct inconsistent with innocence.

generic_facts.theft_mode: meter bypass — registered meter in stopped condition; illegal wire connected into supply cable to load (service cable tampered)
generic_facts.meter_status: meter installed in co-accused wife's name but stopped (reading 17799 KWH)
generic_facts.ownership_evidence: IO recorded neighbours' statements confirming possession; registered consumer claimed to be owner/landlord
generic_facts.defence: bare denial and false implication; no defence evidence; settled civil liability but did not deposit (financial constraints)
generic_facts.outcome: both accused convicted (user u/s 135; registered consumer u/s 135 r/w 150)
